JO.why: Independent judges are the main check between an agency's request and your data. The weaker that check, the easier it is for access to happen without scrutiny.
questions: Agencies can obtain stored data without prior approval from an independent judge or judicial commissioner.
The body that approves access sits inside, or answers to, the executive.
Approvals can cover broad categories or whole programmes rather than named targets.
Providers or affected people have no meaningful way to challenge access in court.

bands.text: Every access needs prior approval from an independent court, limited to named targets, with a real route to challenge it.
Independent prior approval for nearly all access; a few narrow exceptions, such as emergencies, are reviewed by a judge afterwards.
Judicial approval for criminal investigations, but national-security access is approved within the executive or at programme level.
Most access is approved within the executive; courts are involved rarely or in secret, with little chance to challenge.
No independent approval: agencies authorise their own access and it cannot be challenged.

rules: Approval by a prosecutor counts as approval within the executive, unless the prosecutor is shown to be independent of government and the access can be challenged in court.

Executive approval of national-security access stays in 41–60 where criminal access needs a judge and some independent check exists. It moves to 61–80 where high-volume access, such as communications data for all agencies or bulk collection, also has no independent check.

AP.why: This is how much agencies are legally allowed to collect and from whom. The broader the powers, the more of your data falls within scope.
questions: Agencies can collect in bulk, not only data about specific targets.
Agencies can compel service providers to hand over data or give technical assistance.
The grounds for access are broad (such as national security or economic well-being) rather than limited to serious crime.
Foreign nationals' data has fewer protections than citizens' data.

bands.text: Narrow, targeted powers for serious crime only; providers produce specified records and nothing more; everyone's data is equally protected.
Targeted powers with some broader grounds, and limited duties on providers to assist.
Broad national-security grounds and compelled provider assistance, but no bulk collection.
Bulk or programme-level collection with compelled assistance; foreigners' data is less protected.
Effectively unrestricted collection on broad grounds, including direct bulk access to provider systems.

rules: A score of 61 or more needs a documented bulk or programme-level power, set out in law or officially acknowledged. Unconfirmed reports can move a score only within its band.
Foreign-intelligence interception of communications crossing the border, such as cable or signals intelligence, counts as bulk collection in every country alike.

TR.why: Mandated capabilities change the system itself. Once a provider must build access in or weaken encryption, the data is exposed whoever is asking.
questions: Providers can be required to build or maintain interception or access capabilities.
Providers can be required to remove or weaken encryption, or help decrypt data.
Providers must retain data such as metadata or logs for set periods for government use.
Authorities can require changes to products or infrastructure, or advance notice of changes.

bands.text: No mandated access capabilities, no decryption duties and no general data retention.
Limited retention or assistance duties for specific services; no power to require built-in access.
General data retention, and duties to help decrypt where the provider holds the keys.
Providers can be required to build or maintain access capabilities, or to give notice before security changes.
Providers can be ordered to weaken or remove encryption and redesign systems for government access.

rules: A standing duty to keep standard lawful-interception interfaces for executing warrants sits in 41–60. 61–80 is for orders to build new or bespoke capabilities, real-time or direct agency access to networks (including agency equipment in operators' networks), and duties to give notice of security changes.

EX.why: Some laws follow the company rather than the data, so storing data in another country does not take it out of reach.
questions: The law claims access to data stored outside the country.
It applies to providers because of where they are headquartered or incorporated.
It reaches foreign subsidiaries or affiliates through corporate control.
It applies based on the nationality or location of the people the data is about.

bands.text: Powers apply only to data and providers inside the country.
Reach abroad only through treaties such as mutual legal assistance, with the other country involved.
Direct orders to domestic providers for data they hold abroad, subject to court review or comity checks.
Direct claims over data held abroad by domestic companies and their foreign subsidiaries.
Claims over any data connected to its nationals, companies or interests, wherever it is held.

rules: A country that reaches data abroad only through mutual legal assistance or similar treaties scores 21–40, not 0–20.
Authorised remote access to computers or accounts abroad counts as reach over data held abroad: 41–60 with judicial approval, 61–80 without.
The extraterritorial scope of data-protection law (such as GDPR Article 3(2)) is not a government access power. It can raise EX by at most 5 points within its band.

TP.why: Secrecy hides how often powers are used and stops you from knowing your data was accessed, which makes every other risk harder to manage.
questions: The government publishes no meaningful statistics on data-access requests.
Providers can be prevented from disclosing requests, including indefinitely.
Affected people are rarely or never notified after access.
Reports by independent oversight bodies are unpublished or heavily redacted.

bands.text: Regular, detailed statistics; time-limited gag orders; notification once investigations end; published oversight reports.
Published statistics and oversight reports; gag orders are common but reviewable; notification is rare.
Aggregate statistics only, long-lasting gag orders and no notification.
Minimal statistics, indefinite gag orders, and oversight reports that are unpublished or heavily redacted.
No public information about access at all; revealing a request can itself be an offence.

rules: A disclosure offence or gag rule on its own is a 61–80 factor. 81–100 also needs the absence of any official statistics, oversight reporting or notification.

EI.why: An embargo can make providing or using a service unlawful outright, however well the data itself is protected.
questions: A country-wide embargo restricts trade involving this jurisdiction.
The restrictions cover technology, IT or data services specifically.
Several major governments impose restrictions.
Few licences or exceptions are available.
Blocking statutes create conflicting legal obligations.

bands.text: No embargo affects services involving this jurisdiction.
Narrow restrictions on specific goods or technologies, not data services; licences are readily available.
Restrictions on some technology or IT services from at least one major government; licences are possible.
Broad restrictions on technology and data services from several governments, with few licences.
A comprehensive embargo prohibiting nearly all transactions, including data services, with conflicting blocking statutes.

SS.why: Targeted sanctions can prohibit dealing with specific organisations or people, and some penalties reach companies outside the sanctioning country.
questions: Providers, partners or sectors you would rely on are, or are likely to be, on sanctions lists.
Secondary sanctions can penalise foreign companies for dealing with listed parties.
Penalties for violations are severe, such as large fines or criminal liability.
Screening and due-diligence obligations are heavy.
Few exemptions exist for essential or humanitarian services.

bands.text: No relevant organisations or sectors are sanctioned; routine screening is enough.
A few listed parties; standard screening manages the risk.
Key organisations or relevant sectors are sanctioned; enhanced due diligence is needed.
Extensive sanctions on relevant sectors, with a risk of secondary sanctions.
Sweeping sanctions with secondary reach, severe criminal penalties and few exemptions.
